known_limitations: The closed feature owner computes true range as max(high-low,abs(high-previous close),abs(low-previous close)); the first row uses high-low. Fourteen actual completed true ranges are averaged arithmetically, then normalized as 100*SMA14(TR)/closed close. Both the ATR and close must be finite and strictly positive. Immature, invalid or zero observations do not manufacture a ratio or pass availability.

This confirmation is method_atr_percent_available AND NOT(method_atr_percent>0.10). Thus 0.10 percent equality may continue, while greater values WAIT; 0.10 percent is not a fraction of 0.10, ten percent, an absolute price distance, or an account-risk percentage. It never creates a direction or entry.

TradingView's normalization formula uses RMA14 ATR. Preserving the existing closed SMA14 owner is an explicit lab smoothing adaptation, not a change to management ATR or an assertion of exact publisher-indicator equivalence. The fixed 0.10 percent cap and trend-up/New York/normal-volatility research scope are lab hypotheses; no optimal search, calibration or profitability is asserted.

The explicit New York scope is a new execution question chosen after already-seen archive opportunity inspection, not untouched validation or an expansion/rewriting of old London-only revisions. The method applies only where the original strategy candidate reaches the existing entry decision path; all other context, data, account, risk, execution and admission guards remain mandatory.

Original closed OHLC and observation time bind the ratio. CSV-supplied method fields, future suffixes, modeled execution spread and censored outcomes cannot supply missing observations. Physical stops, targets, size, costs, leverage and external risk limits are unchanged.

This source-backed executable rule and its software tests are not independent economic qualification, useful causal skill, Master status, credit, promotion or paper/live authority. Archive outcomes retain their reused-data status; 2026 and later data remain paper-only.
